content: For P vs NP, I'd expect any genuine solution now to come with a formalized proof either at release time or shortly thereafter. This contrasts with Poincaré where it took a long time for there to be consensus, pre-Lean, that Perelman had solved the problem. The only Millennium Prize Problems now where Lean might not enable correctness to be established quickly are probably Yang-Mills (see previous discussions of not having a sufficiently precise statement to formalize exactly what does or does not count as a solution) and any cases where a solution turns out to depend on an enormous computation (considering that people have done huge computations related to RH and BSD, we can hardly rule out the possibility that an eventual solution is found that depends on such a computation, so that only a conditional formalization is possible).

For P vs NP, the formalization would have to be carefully studied. It is easy to make subtle mistakes in defining TMs, and as we learnt a few months ago, seemingly equivalent textbook definitions can turn out to be non-equivalent (well… one of them was plain wrong).

Joseph Myers said:

I think it's reasonable for complexity classes of counting problems (such as #P) to use a separate definition from complexity classes of decision problems.

It is indeed valid. But then I'd call it DecisionComplexityClasses. The most general formulation would of course use functions since they can be specialized into decision, function, and counting cases
Feel free to open a PR!
But there are also lots of complexity classes that can't be defined in terms of functions (e.g. sampling problems, interactive problems), so it's not like that is the be-all end-all.

I've also seen several books that define a "complexity class" to be a more restrictive notion than just "set of languages", e.g. to be a proper "complexity class" it has to have some additional properties like being closed under finite transductions or closed under string homomorphisms.
I have no objection to ComplexityClass being renamed to something like DecisionComplexityClass.

WRT to the possibility of subtle mistakes, this definitely worries me. I think the best cure for that (beyond staring intently at the code, and asking powerful LLMs to stare at the code) is probably to develop the theory more and make sure we can prove the theorems we expect to be able to prove. To this end, I think a step we might want to consider is making formal-conjectures depend on cslib and putting definitions of these concepts there.

Alex Meiburg said:

I've also seen several books that define a "complexity class" to be a more restrictive notion than just "set of languages", e.g. to be a proper "complexity class" it has to have some additional properties like being closed under finite transductions or closed under string homomorphisms.

Yeah, this is an interesting point, and I have sometimes considered things like it. I guess the thing that gives me pause is: for complexity classes X that we might want to define, how easy is it to prove that compositions of finite transductions with complexity class X is themselves in X, in order to be able to define / prove that X is a valid complexity class. When I think of P for example, we have no proof in mathlib that compositions of polytime functions are polytime. We do have such a proof in CSLib, but I used LLM assistance to write that proof, and it felt like it would have been hard to write without such assistance. IDK how much harder it will be to prove this for other classes, but I don't want defining new classes to be harder than it has to be.
Okay. So a renaming PR for now?

For your information, P vs. NP problem can be formulated in less than 50 lines (and in a reasonably natural way, not just through weird trick) #general > cook levin, np completeness of SAT @ 💬 . See also #CSLib > Cobham's axioms .

I think this form of presentation should be on formal-cojectures.

I am aware of the multiple formalisms of polytime computation. But there is a very good reason people don’t use them in complexity theory. They don’t have a rich theory of reductions, algorithms, and lower bounds. I can’t say what should or should not be in FC. Nor can I predict how a P vs NP resolution would come about. But the standard formalism(s) are likely to be in the proof path.
